reference: The radio is the GTA ad break — traditionally the crudest, most satirical material in a game like this. The apartment is a man alone in a room talking to himself.
diagnosis: The radio is the biggest missed opportunity in the game. Ad-break parody is where a satire like this is supposed to be filthiest, and instead the announcer is doing warm, flattering, real-radio copy — 'the only station where every host thinks they're the smartest person in the building… and somehow they are' is a compliment, not a joke. There is no product being sold badly, no lawyer's disclaimer read at four hundred words a minute, no local business run by an obvious criminal. Separately, the apartment has an outright doctrine violation: `vo.door.hint.piss.1` has the character say 'hold F' out loud. The tone doc's own rule is that a character speaks and the screen clarifies afterwards, never the character reading the button. And the one genuinely adult beat in the game — Margo and the zip — is written coy.

lines.current: Stand over it, hold F, and stop overthinking it.
lines.why: DOCTRINE VIOLATION — the character speaks the keybind. The tone doc names this exact failure: the character speaks first, the HUD clarifies in the onDone. Every variant below leaves the button to the screen.
lines.house: It's a toilet. I've done this before. I've done this thousands of times.
lines.tarantino: It's a toilet. I have used a toilet every day of my life since I was three years old and somehow this one is a decision.
lines.mcdonagh: It's a jacks. I've used a jacks. Why am I stood here thinkin' about it.
lines.houser: It's a toilet. I have a mortgage and a criminal record and I am standing here strategising about a toilet.
lines.coen: It's a toilet. I know how to do this. I've just — okay. Here we go.

lines.current: The nightstand. There is a drawer in the nightstand.
lines.why: An interactable-object label with a voice on it. Nobody describes their own furniture to themselves.
lines.house: Clothes. There were clothes. They were in the nightstand and I was wearing some of them.
lines.tarantino: The nightstand. There's a drawer in it. There's been a drawer in it for four years and I have never once opened it sober.
lines.mcdonagh: The nightstand. There's a drawer. I know there's a drawer, I've been avoidin' it.
lines.houser: Nightstand. There's a drawer. I keep everything in there I'd rather not explain to anyone.
lines.coen: The nightstand. There's a drawer there. I put things in it. That's where things go.

lines.current: Through the north door. Get in it.
lines.why: 'North door' is a map callout. A man in his own apartment does not navigate by compass.
lines.house: Shower. I smell like the inside of somebody's car.
lines.tarantino: Shower. I smell like a car. Not my car. Somebody else's car, which is worse.
lines.mcdonagh: A shower. I smell like the inside of a car that isn't mine.
lines.houser: Shower. I currently smell like a rental vehicle and a decision I regret.
lines.coen: I should shower. I smell like — yeah. I should shower.

lines.current: The bank is done. The next call is not here yet.
lines.why: A system gate message wearing dialogue clothing. He is describing the game's state machine.
lines.house: Bank's done. Nobody's called. And when nobody calls, you sit down.
lines.tarantino: The bank's done. Nobody's called. And in this business, nobody calling is either the best week of your life or the last one, and you don't find out which until it's over.
lines.mcdonagh: The bank's done and nobody's rung. And that's either grand or it's very bad, and there's no way of knowin' till it's too late.
lines.houser: Bank's closed out. No follow-up. Which in this organization means either I did it right or somebody's currently deciding about me.
lines.coen: The bank's done. Nobody's called. That's either good or it isn't. Hard to say.

lines.current: Lou said seven. The invitation still has to land.
lines.why: Same gate-check problem — 'has to land' is production language, not his.
lines.house: Lou said seven. It's not seven. You don't show up early to a thing like that.
lines.tarantino: Lou said seven. It's not seven. And nobody in the history of this family has ever been rewarded for showing up early to something like this.
lines.mcdonagh: Lou said seven. It's not seven. You don't turn up early to that kind of thing, you look desperate.
lines.houser: Lou said seven. It's not seven. Arriving early to your own initiation reads as eager, and eager is how people get given the bad jobs.
lines.coen: Lou said seven. It's not seven yet. So.

lines.why: Vague nostalgia filler, sitting right next to the excellent 'Everyone in that picture owes me money'.
lines.house: Three of them in that photo are dead and one of them owes me forty bucks.
lines.tarantino: Look at that. Nobody in that picture knew what was coming. That's what a photograph is, when you get down to it. It's a room full of people who don't know yet.
lines.mcdonagh: God, look at that. Half of them are dead and the other half stopped ringin'.
lines.houser: Great night. Two of those people are incarcerated and one of them is a witness, so it's really more of a document now.
lines.coen: Huh. That was a good time. That was — yeah. That was a while ago now.

lines.current: Let it be known: that was a great time.
lines.why: Could describe any photograph ever taken. No specificity, no crudeness, no personality.
lines.house: That was the last good night before everything got complicated.
lines.tarantino: That was a great night. That was the last one where nobody at the table had done anything you couldn't come back from.
lines.mcdonagh: That was a great night, that was. Last one before it all went sideways, mind.
lines.houser: Great night. Everyone in that picture still had a clean record and a functioning liver.
lines.coen: That was a great time. That was before all the — well. It was before.

lines.current: The zip. Come here. That is not a request — I am not sleeping in this dress.
lines.why: OWNER DECISION NEEDED — this is the game's one adult beat and it is written coy. The line is already good (the 'not a request' is right); what it lacks is that Margo is in complete control and enjoying it. The variants below raise the heat without going graphic — pick a level and I'll match the rest of the scene to it.
lines.house: The zip. Come here. That's not a request, and don't take all night about it — I've been thinking about this since the second course.
lines.tarantino: The zip. Come here. And I want to be clear about something before you touch it: this is not you getting lucky. This is me deciding, at a table, about two hours ago, and you catching up.
lines.mcdonagh: The zip. Come here. That's not a request. And take your time with it, because I've been in this bloody thing since six and I intend to enjoy gettin' out of it.
lines.houser: The zip. Come here. That's not a request. I've had a plan since the appetiser and you are currently the only part of it running behind.
lines.coen: The zip. Come here. That's not — I'm not asking. I've been in this dress since six and I'm done with it.

lines.current: Keep doing work like that and there is a bright future for you here.
lines.why: A middle manager's pep talk from a mob boss, immediately after a violent job. 'Bright future' drains every drop of menace out of the moment.
lines.house: Keep doing work like that and you'll be somebody in this family. Keep doing it too well and you'll be somebody they talk about.
lines.tarantino: Keep working like that and you'll go a long way here. And I want you to hear both halves of that, because a long way in this family is a long way from where you started, and there's no road back down it.
lines.mcdonagh: Keep doin' work like that and you'll do well here. And that's a warnin' as much as anythin', but take it however suits you.
lines.houser: Keep performing like that and there's a real path for you in this organization. There's also a shorter one. Both of them are paths.
lines.coen: You keep doing work like that, you'll do all right here. That's not nothing. That's about the most anybody gets told.

lines.current: I have a package for you, and I need it handled tonight.
lines.why: Generic mob-boss phrasing with none of the specific menace of Lou's better lines.
lines.house: There's a thing here with your name on it and it stops being useful at midnight.
lines.tarantino: I've got something here for you, and it's got a clock on it. Not a metaphor. An actual clock. It stops mattering at midnight and after that it's just a problem I own.
lines.mcdonagh: I've a thing here for you and it needs doin' tonight. Not tomorrow. Tonight, before it turns into somethin' worse.
lines.houser: I have an item with a very short shelf life and your name attached to it. Tonight, or it becomes a liability with my name attached to it.
lines.coen: I've got a package for you. It needs handling tonight. Not tomorrow. That's the part that matters.

lines.current: Tonight is the night. Do not make other plans.
lines.why: Stock action-movie opener on a major story gate.
lines.house: Tonight's the night. Whatever else you had on, you didn't.
lines.tarantino: Tonight's the night. Whatever else you had planned — and I know you had nothing planned, but on the off chance — you didn't.
lines.mcdonagh: Tonight's the night. Whatever else you'd on, you hadn't.
lines.houser: Tonight's the night. Everything else in your calendar has been cancelled by me, on your behalf, without consultation.
lines.coen: Tonight's the night. Don't make any other plans. Not that you had any.

lines.current: Shower, shave, wear something clean. This one is about you, Tony.
lines.why: 'This one is about you, Tony' is a sports-movie mentor speech. The instruction half is great; the sentiment half is too tender for this world.
lines.house: Shower, shave, wear something clean. Everybody in that room is going to be looking at you and most of them are hoping you screw it up.
lines.tarantino: Shower. Shave. Wear something clean. And I mean clean — every man in that room is going to look at you for exactly four seconds and decide something, and you don't get a second four seconds.
lines.mcdonagh: Shower, shave, wear somethin' clean. Every fella in that room'll look at you for four seconds and make his mind up forever. That's how it works and it's not fair and there it is.
lines.houser: Shower, shave, wear something clean. This is a first impression with a room full of people who make permanent decisions in under five seconds.
lines.coen: Shower, shave, put on something clean. This one's about you. That's — that's not always a good thing, but it's about you.

lines.current: You're locked in to Uncle Squatch Beats. Ninety eight point eight. Take it easy.
lines.why: A stock real-radio sign-off. It is the weakest of the three station idents it sits beside, and station idents are free personality.
lines.house: Uncle Squatch Beats. Ninety eight point eight. Nobody here is qualified and nobody here is leaving.
lines.tarantino: Uncle Squatch Beats. Ninety eight point eight. Same six records, same guy, same chair. I haven't been outside since March.
lines.mcdonagh: Uncle Squatch Beats. Ninety eight point eight. I've been in this room eleven hours and I've stopped noticin' the smell.
lines.houser: Uncle Squatch Beats. Ninety eight point eight. Legally distinct from every other station, according to a letter we received.
lines.coen: Uncle Squatch Beats. Ninety eight point eight. Take it easy. There's not a lot else to do.

lines.current: The only station where every host thinks they're the smartest person in the building… and somehow they are.
lines.why: A compliment dressed as a joke. GTA-style station promo works by being proudly, specifically terrible about itself.
lines.house: The only station where every host thinks he's the smartest man in the building, and the building is a trailer, and there is one host.
lines.tarantino: The only station where every host believes he's the smartest man in the building. There are two of us. The other one is a vending machine.
lines.mcdonagh: The only station where every host thinks he's the cleverest fella in the buildin'. There's the one of us. And I'm not sure about him.
lines.houser: The only station where every host is convinced he's the smartest man in the building, which is technically true, because we let the other one go in April.
lines.coen: The only station where every host thinks he's the smartest guy in the building. And, you know. There's only the one of them.

lines.current: Tired of boring radio stations that care about "facts" and "professionalism"?
lines.why: A generic strawman ad opener. Nothing about it is Squatch, and it names its own joke with scare quotes.
lines.house: Tired of radio stations that check things? Stations with lawyers? Stations that stop talking when the phone rings?
lines.tarantino: You tired of stations that check things? Stations with a legal department? A station where a man in a suit walks in and says 'we can't say that on air'? We had one of those. He doesn't work here now. Nobody knows where he went.
lines.mcdonagh: Are you sick of stations that check their facts? That have a lawyer? That stop talkin' when somethin' bad happens? We've none of that. We've none of any of it.
lines.houser: Fed up with radio that fact-checks, apologises, and issues corrections? We have never issued a correction. Not because we're right. We just don't do it.
lines.coen: You tired of stations that care about facts? Professionalism? We don't have either one. We had a guy. He left.

lines.current: Then tune your dial to 97.8… THE SQUATCH!
lines.why: Boilerplate CTA, interchangeable with any real station.
lines.house: Then get on ninety seven point eight. THE SQUATCH. We are legally required to say the number twice and nothing else.
lines.tarantino: Then it's ninety seven point eight. THE SQUATCH. Say it out loud. Say it in a room with other people. Watch what happens to their faces.
lines.mcdonagh: Then it's ninety seven point eight. THE SQUATCH. There's nowhere else. There's literally nowhere else on the dial out here.
lines.houser: Then it's ninety seven point eight. THE SQUATCH. The only station in this valley, which is not a boast, it's a geographical fact and a tragedy.
lines.coen: So that's ninety seven point eight. THE SQUATCH. It's the only one that comes in out here, anyway.

lines.current: The Squatch Meeting is Wednesday. Tomorrow. Seven in the evening.
lines.why: A UI objective marker read on air. Story reminders through the radio are a great idea — this one just has no radio in it.
lines.house: The Squatch Meeting is Wednesday. Tomorrow. Seven in the evening. We are not told what it is. We are told to say it.
lines.tarantino: The Squatch Meeting is Wednesday. Tomorrow. Seven in the evening. That's all the information on the card. I've asked. I've asked three times. There's no more card.
lines.mcdonagh: The Squatch Meetin' is Wednesday. Tomorrow. Seven in the evenin'. That's all that's on the page and I'll not be takin' questions.
lines.houser: The Squatch Meeting is Wednesday. Tomorrow. Seven p.m. This announcement has been paid for in cash by a man who would not give his name and would not sit down.
lines.coen: The Squatch Meeting is Wednesday. That's tomorrow. Seven in the evening. That's what it says here.

newMaterial.note: The ad break is the one place the doctrine's 'comedy lives in the world' rule gives you a free hand — nobody in an ad is a character in a scene, so it can be as crude as you like. There are 33 unrecorded announcer lines in the queue; these are pitches for what to put in them, not fixes to existing lines.
pitches: SQUATCH DENTAL — a dental practice for a species with forty teeth and no insurance. 'We are not dentists. We have been told we cannot say we are dentists. We are men with the equipment of dentists.' Closing disclaimer read at four hundred words a minute.

LOU'S JERKY — a straight, warm, family-business ad for the jerky brand, with one sentence near the end that makes it clear what the jerky is. Played completely straight. The doctrine's whole method, in thirty seconds.
THE ATTORNEY — a personal injury ad by a lawyer who is visibly a criminal defence attorney pretending to do personal injury. 'Have you been hurt? Have you hurt somebody? Either one. Call the number.'
THE PUBLIC SERVICE ANNOUNCEMENT — a county safety notice about not feeding the sasquatches, read by an announcer who is plainly a sasquatch and increasingly offended by the copy.
THE DATING LINE — a phone service, read in the tone of a warm romantic ad, with escalating clarifications about what is and is not covered, ending in a full minute of legal disclaimer about fur.
THE GYM — 'RESULTS PHYSICAL' — for a species that is already eight feet tall. Entirely about the emotional insecurity of very large men. Nobody in it lifts anything.

THE CAR DEALERSHIP — a man screaming about financing at a volume that becomes physically alarming, who at the end of the ad, at normal volume, quietly asks the listener to come and see him because he is in trouble.
THE OVERNIGHT AUTOMATION — the station's unmanned overnight, where the same six pre-recorded links play out of order and slowly reveal that the announcer recorded them under duress.

reference: The Silver Room is the supper-club date — the mob-restaurant scene. Silver Pines is the round of golf where the real conversation happens.
diagnosis: Two different failures wearing the same coat. Margo is written razor-sharp for two hundred lines and then hands the player a polite dinner-date sign-off ('Thank you for dinner. The band was excellent.') at the one moment the scene needs heat. And the Prospect — a man the entire room is visibly afraid of — orders drinks like a hotel guest. 'We're fine.' 'We're alright.' 'Beer's fine.' 'Same again, when you get a second.' The sibling line 'Two cubes, I'm not an animal' proves the scene knows exactly how this man talks; he just stops talking that way whenever a waiter appears. On the course, Eric's caddie lines have collapsed into UI toasts — 'You have clubs.' 'You have a shot.' 'You have selected a driver.' — which is the game narrating itself in a man's voice.

lines.current: I'm going to let them call me a car. Thank you for dinner. The band was excellent.
lines.why: The scene's biggest turn, and Margo suddenly speaks like a wedding thank-you card. This is the version where she says no — it should still be HER saying no, with a blade in it.
lines.house: I'm going to let them call me a car. And you're going to let me, and neither of us is going to say anything clever about it.
lines.tarantino: I'm going to let them call me a car. Not because the night went badly. It didn't. But I've watched every man in this room look at you twice, and I know exactly what that means, and I'd like to go home before I stop caring what it means.
lines.mcdonagh: I'll let them call me a car. It was a lovely dinner and you're a lovely fella and there's somethin' badly wrong with you, and I'd rather find out what on a night I've less drink in me.
lines.houser: I'm going to let them call me a car. Dinner was excellent, the band was fine, and you are a series of red flags in a very good jacket.
lines.coen: I'm going to let them call me a car. It was a nice dinner. I mean that. It's not a — it's not a thing about you.

lines.why: Stock politeness from the sharpest voice in the game.
lines.house: That's the first kind thing anybody's done in this room all night.
lines.tarantino: That's kind. Which is a strange word to use about anything that happens in this building, but there it is.
lines.mcdonagh: That's kind of you. And I'll say that now, before I find out what it costs.
lines.houser: That's kind. In my experience kind comes with an invoice, so I'll wait for the invoice.
lines.coen: That's kind. Thank you. People aren't, generally.

lines.current: You want to come back for a drink?
lines.why: A dating-app line from a man who has spent the whole evening being the most dangerous person in the room. It should be direct and slightly alarming, which is what she likes about him.
lines.house: Come back with me. There's a bottle I've been saving for a reason I couldn't name until about an hour ago.
lines.tarantino: Come back with me. I'm not going to dress it up. There's a bottle, there's a record player that mostly works, and there's the fact that I've been thinking about this since the second course.
lines.mcdonagh: Come back with me. I'll not pretend it's about a drink. There is a drink. But it's not about the drink.
lines.houser: Come back to mine. I have exactly one good bottle, one clean glass, and no plan beyond that, and I'd rather be honest about the inventory.
lines.coen: You want to come back? For a drink, or — I mean. You know what I'm asking. I'd rather just ask it.

lines.current: The night doesn't have to end here.
lines.why: A rom-com line. Sanitised in a way nothing else in this scene is.
lines.house: I'm not ready for this to be over and I'm too old to pretend otherwise.
lines.tarantino: The night doesn't have to end here. And I want you to notice I said that out loud, in a room full of men who work for my uncle, which should tell you how much I mean it.
lines.mcdonagh: I don't want the night to end. There. That's me said it, and I'll be mortified about it later.
lines.houser: I don't want this to end here. And I'm aware that's the least sophisticated thing I've said all evening.
lines.coen: The night doesn't have to end. It could keep going. I'd like it to keep going.

lines.current: I'll get you a car. This was good.
lines.why: 'This was good' is a non-summary of an entire evening built on specific banter. It is the sound of a man who has stopped trying.
lines.house: I'll get you a car. And for what it's worth — that's the best night I've had in a building I'm allowed in.
lines.tarantino: I'll get you a car. And I want to say one true thing before you get in it: that's the best three hours I've had in about four years, and I've had some very expensive hours.
lines.mcdonagh: I'll get you a car. And that was the best night I've had in a long while, and I'll not be sayin' it twice.
lines.houser: I'll have a car brought round. And on the record — that was the most fun I've had somewhere I didn't have to check the exits.
lines.coen: I'll get you a car. That was — that was a good night. I'd like to say something better than that, but that's what I've got.

lines.why: Functional. The confidence is right; the personality is missing.
lines.house: Car's outside. It's been outside an hour. I was optimistic.
lines.tarantino: Car's outside. It's been outside since the appetiser, which I realise says something about me that I'm not going to examine tonight.
lines.mcdonagh: Car's outside. It's been outside the whole time. I'd it waitin'. That's how sure of meself I was, God help me.
lines.houser: Car's outside. It has been outside for ninety minutes. That's either confidence or a character flaw, and I've stopped keeping them separate.
lines.coen: Car's out front. It's been there a while. I had it wait.

lines.why: A polite customer in a room that is visibly afraid of him. Every waiter interaction in this scene is written this way and they all need the same fix.
lines.house: We're looked after. Go be somewhere else for twenty minutes.
lines.tarantino: We're looked after. And I'd take it as a personal kindness if the next twenty minutes happened without you in them.
lines.mcdonagh: We're grand. Off you go now. Go and hover at someone else.
lines.houser: We're taken care of. Give us twenty minutes of not existing and there's something in it for you.
lines.coen: We're looked after, thanks. We're fine. You can — yeah. Thank you.

lines.current: Same again, when you get a second.
lines.why: 'When you get a second' undercuts the feared-mobster status the whole scene has been building.
lines.house: Same again. You've got a second.
lines.tarantino: Same again. And I know you're busy. I've watched you be busy at three other tables. You've got a second.
lines.mcdonagh: Same again. And don't be givin' me the face, I can see the face.
lines.houser: Same again. And I'd like it to arrive before the conversation improves, not after.
lines.coen: Same again, please. Whenever. No rush. Well — some rush.

lines.why: Generic drink order sitting next to 'Two cubes, I'm not an animal' — the scene's own proof of how good these can be.
lines.house: Beer. Whatever's coldest. I'm not here to have a conversation about it.
lines.tarantino: Beer. Cold. In a glass that hasn't got anybody's mouth-print on it, which I'm told is a big ask in this town.
lines.mcdonagh: A beer. Whatever's coldest. And don't be tellin' me about it, I don't want the story of it.
lines.houser: Beer. Domestic. Cold. I'm not paying eleven dollars to be educated about hops tonight.
lines.coen: A beer's fine. Whatever you've got. I'm easy on that.

lines.why: Placeholder. Reused verbatim at vo.silver.player.servicebar.open.1eyqtkv, which doubles the damage — one flat line saying itself twice in one scene.
lines.house: We're fine. And if we stop being fine, you'll know, because it'll be loud.
lines.tarantino: We're fine. And when we're not fine, I promise you'll be the second to know.
lines.mcdonagh: We're grand. If we stop bein' grand you'll hear about it from across the room.
lines.houser: We're fine. If that changes it'll change dramatically and you'll have plenty of warning.
lines.coen: We're fine. Thanks. We're all set here.

lines.why: The duplicate. Give it a different mouth-feel so the player never hears the same nothing twice.
lines.house: Nothing from the bar. We're two drinks past sensible already.
lines.tarantino: Nothing from the bar. We're two past the point where anything I order is a good decision.
lines.mcdonagh: Nothin' from the bar. We're well past the drink that made sense.
lines.houser: Nothing from the bar. We've comfortably exceeded the responsible allocation.
lines.coen: We're all set. Nothing from the bar. Thank you, though.

lines.why: Customer-service filler with no edge.
lines.house: We're good. Keep it running and keep your eyes on the door, not on us.
lines.tarantino: We're good. Keep it running. And whatever you see in that mirror tonight, you saw it in a different car.
lines.mcdonagh: We're grand. Keep her runnin'. And whatever you see, you didn't.
lines.houser: We're good. Engine on, radio off, eyes forward. You're transport, not company.
lines.coen: Thanks, we're good. Just keep it running, if you don't mind.

lines.why: The third variation on the same nothing. Part of a systemic fix, not a one-line fix.
lines.house: We're alright. Come back when one of us looks unhappy.
lines.tarantino: We're alright. Come back when somebody at this table looks like they need saving.
lines.mcdonagh: We're alright. Come back when one of us has a face on.
lines.houser: We're alright. Circle back when the mood shifts, you'll be able to tell.
lines.coen: We're alright, thanks. We'll wave if we need anything.

lines.why: The flattest of three toast options; its siblings land specific callbacks and this one is a shrug.
lines.house: To the third number. Whatever it turns out to be, and whoever ends up paying for it.
lines.tarantino: To the third number. I don't know what it is yet. Neither do you. That's the whole reason it's worth drinking to.
lines.mcdonagh: To the third number. Nobody knows what it is. That's the beauty of it and also the problem.
lines.houser: To the third number, which I'm told is where the real money is and where all the arrests happen.
lines.coen: To the third number. Whatever that ends up being. Here's to it.

lines.current: Thank you. That's all. Thank you.
lines.why: Repetitive and flat, with none of Margo's bite. Reads like a placeholder that never got written.
lines.house: Thank you. That's genuinely all I need, and I'd like to be left with it.
lines.tarantino: Thank you. That's all. And I mean all — I've been in this room forty minutes and every single person in it has asked me if I need something.
lines.mcdonagh: Thank you. That's the lot. Now go away before you ask me again, the pair of yiz keep askin' me.
lines.houser: Thank you. That's everything. This is the fourth time somebody's checked on me and I'm starting to feel like a suspect.
lines.coen: Thank you. That's all. I appreciate it. I do.

lines.why: Sincere but generic, and it flattens the wary intelligence she has everywhere else.
lines.house: Thank you. And I don't say that in here, so mark the day.
lines.tarantino: Thank you. Genuinely. And I want you to understand I've said thank you twice in this building in six years, and you've now had both of them.
lines.mcdonagh: Thank you. Genuinely, now. And I don't do genuinely, so enjoy it while it's here.
lines.houser: Thank you. Sincerely. Which is not a mode I operate in professionally, so make a note.
lines.coen: Thank you. Really. I mean that. I don't say it much.

lines.why: A UI toast in a man's mouth. This is the HUD-instruction failure the tone doc names explicitly, and Eric is written with dry wit everywhere else.
lines.house: Driver. Bold. On this hole. All right.
lines.tarantino: The driver. Okay. On a par three. I'm not going to say anything, I'm just going to stand back here and watch.
lines.mcdonagh: The driver, is it. On this hole. Grand. I'll stand well back so.
lines.houser: You've gone with the driver. That's an aggressive choice for a man who couldn't find the first tee.
lines.coen: That's the driver. Huh. Okay. That's a choice.

lines.why: System message. Same failure family as the line above — the game telling the player his inventory using a character.
lines.house: Those are clubs. Somebody paid a lot for them and it wasn't you.
lines.tarantino: Those are clubs. Real ones. Somebody paid four thousand dollars for those and it was not you, and I want you to carry that knowledge into your swing.
lines.mcdonagh: Them's clubs. Proper ones. Someone paid a fortune for them and it wasn't you, so mind them.
lines.houser: You've got clubs. Borrowed clubs. Which means every mistake you make today belongs to somebody else.
lines.coen: Those are your clubs there. They're good ones. They're not yours, but they're good ones.

lines.why: Third UI toast from the same character. Eric needs a pass across the whole hole, not three separate patches.
lines.house: You've got a shot. Not a good one. But a shot.
lines.tarantino: You've got a shot. I want to be careful how I say this — you have a shot the way a man falling off a roof has a plan.
lines.mcdonagh: You've a shot. It's not a good shot. But it's a shot, and that's more than you had a minute ago.
lines.houser: You have a shot. Whether you have the swing is a separate conversation we'll have afterwards.
lines.coen: You've got a shot there. It's not much of one. But it's there.

lines.why: Textbook mission-accept boilerplate. Could be any character in any genre.
lines.house: Got it. I still don't know why I'm here, but got it.
lines.tarantino: Understood. I don't understand any of it, but I understand that I'm supposed to say understood.
lines.mcdonagh: Understood. I've not a clue what's happenin', but understood.
lines.houser: Understood. Which is not the same as informed, but I've learned not to push.
lines.coen: Understood. I think. I'll go along with it.

lines.why: Hollow bravado cliché.
lines.house: I'm ready. I've got no idea what for, but I'm ready.
lines.tarantino: I'm ready. Which is a strange thing to be, on a golf course, in a borrowed shirt, with a man I've met twice.
lines.mcdonagh: I'm ready. Ready for what, I couldn't tell you, but I'm ready.
lines.houser: I'm ready. In the sense that I'm here and I've stopped asking questions.
lines.coen: I'm ready. I guess. Sure.

lines.why: Completely generic subordinate-to-boss line with no edge for an ambitious prospect.
lines.house: I did what you asked. All of it. Including the part you didn't say out loud.
lines.tarantino: I did what you asked. And then I did the part you didn't ask for but definitely wanted, which I'd like noted somewhere.
lines.mcdonagh: I did what you asked. And the bit you didn't ask for and were hopin' I'd do anyway. I did that too.
lines.houser: I did what was asked. And the unasked part, which is where the real work always is and where nobody ever looks.
lines.coen: I did what you asked. All of it. I didn't ask any questions about it, either.

lines.why: Vague placeholder that contributes nothing to the beat.
lines.house: I came back. That's the part that should worry you.
lines.tarantino: I came back. And I want you to sit with that for a second, because a smarter man wouldn't have.
lines.mcdonagh: I came back. Which says more about me than it does about you, and neither of us should be happy about it.
lines.houser: I came back. Voluntarily. That's either loyalty or a diagnosis.
lines.coen: I came back. I don't know that I had to. But I did.

lines.why: Stock dialogue-menu phrasing where the character could be guarded and sharp.
lines.house: Is this a test? Because everything's been a test and nobody tells me the results.
lines.tarantino: Is this another test? Because so far everything's been a test, nobody's ever told me the score, and I'm starting to think that's the test.
lines.mcdonagh: Is this another test? Everythin's a test with you lot. Do I ever pass? Has anyone ever passed?
lines.houser: Is this another evaluation? Because I've been continuously assessed for eleven weeks and nobody's shared a single metric with me.
lines.coen: Is this a test? It seems like a test. Everything's been a test so far.

lines.why: Could belong to any character in any scene.
lines.house: What happens then? To me, specifically.
lines.tarantino: What happens then. And I'm asking about me specifically, not the general case.
lines.mcdonagh: And what happens then? To me. Not to everyone. To me.
lines.houser: What's the outcome? And I'd like it in terms of what happens to me, not to the organization.
lines.coen: What happens then? I'm just trying to get a picture of it.

lines.current: And if it doesn't go well?
lines.why: Generic stakes-question phrasing.
lines.house: And if it goes bad? Do I find out, or does somebody else find out about me?
lines.tarantino: And if it goes badly? I'm asking because in my experience there's two versions of badly, and only one of them involves me still being around to hear about it.
lines.mcdonagh: And if it goes wrong? Do I hear about it, or does someone hear about me?
lines.houser: And if it fails? Is that a conversation, or is that a phone call somebody else receives about me?
lines.coen: And if it doesn't go well? What does that look like? For me.

lines.why: Flavourless humility that does nothing the scene needs.
lines.house: I got lucky. I'd rather be lucky here than good anywhere else.
lines.tarantino: I got lucky. And I've decided I'm fine with that. Lucky's a skill nobody can take off you because nobody can prove you had it.
lines.mcdonagh: I got lucky. And I'd rather be lucky than good, because good runs out.
lines.houser: I got lucky. Which in this organization is functionally identical to being talented and considerably cheaper.
lines.coen: I got lucky. That's all that was. I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

lines.why: Stock disbelief with no personality attached.
lines.house: That's it? That's the whole thing? I got dressed for that?
lines.tarantino: That's it? That's the whole thing? I ironed a shirt.
lines.mcdonagh: That's it? That's the whole of it? I've a shirt on and everythin'.
lines.houser: That's it? I cleared my morning and rented shoes for that.
lines.coen: That's it? Huh. Okay. I thought there'd be more to it.

lines.why: Generic straight-man setup with no specific voice.
lines.house: I thought this was work. Nobody said bring shoes.
lines.tarantino: I thought this was work. I brought a jacket. There's a man over there in shorts drinking a gin and tonic at ten in the morning.
lines.mcdonagh: I thought this was work. I've a jacket on. There's a fella over there in shorts with a drink in him and it's ten in the mornin'.
lines.houser: I was told this was work. I've dressed for a meeting and arrived at a leisure activity, which I'm choosing to find informative.
lines.coen: I thought this was work. I brought a jacket and everything.

reference: The Godfather — the Louis Restaurant sit-down. Sal is Sollozzo, McClawsky is the bought cop, the Prospect is Michael. The gun is behind the cistern.
diagnosis: The flattest writing in the game. Every line is a summary of a feeling rather than a thing a person says. 'Business disagreement.' 'You hit me.' 'You were being difficult.' Nobody in a room where somebody is about to be shot in the face talks in four-word abstractions. The scene has no smell, no body, no money in it. Sal should be charming and obscene at once — he is asking a kid to sell his family and he does it like a man ordering veal. McClawsky is a cop on the take who despises everyone at the table including himself.

lines.why: Bellhop politeness from a bent cop. He is escorting a kid to a table where he expects him to fold; that should be in his mouth.
lines.house: Move, ape. He's been sat in there forty minutes with nothing in front of him but a glass of water and his own opinions.
lines.tarantino: Forty minutes he's been in that booth. No food, no paper, nothing to look at. You know what a man does with forty empty minutes? He starts deciding things. Let's get in there before he finishes.
lines.mcdonagh: Come on to fuck. He gets worse the longer he sits, and he started out fairly bad.
lines.houser: Let's go, big man. Table's under a name neither of us can spell, the meter's running, and I've got a wife who thinks I'm at a prayer group.
lines.coen: They're waiting on you. I don't like to be the one to say it. But they have been waiting a while now, and it's the kind of thing that gets noticed.

lines.current: The Sasquatches are making business difficult.
lines.why: A press release. Sal wants to sound reasonable, but 'difficult' costs him nothing to say and tells the player nothing about what he actually wants.
lines.house: Your family is costing me money in a way I can't put on a page. Every week I write a number down and every week your uncle makes it smaller with his hands.
lines.tarantino: You know what I like about your people? Commitment. Genuine, unreasonable commitment. I've got two docks, four routes, and a man in Tacoma who counts for me, and every one of them has been made stupid by sasquatches who will not take a phone call. That's not war. War I understand. That's just bad manners with a body count.
lines.mcdonagh: Your lot are ruinin' me. Not beatin' me, mind. Ruinin' me. There's a difference and it's mostly paperwork.
lines.houser: Let me be transparent with you, because I value transparency. Your family is a market inefficiency. You're sitting on distribution you don't understand, running it like a hobby, and I'm the one man in this city willing to professionalize it before somebody less friendly does it for free.
lines.coen: Things have been difficult. Business-wise. I don't want to overstate it. But I've had to have conversations I'd rather not have had, and I'd say that's on your family, more or less.

lines.why: Statement of fact with no injury in it. The kid watched his people get shot; this reads like a customer-service complaint.
lines.house: You put four in my uncle outside a fruit stand and now you want to talk about routes.
lines.tarantino: See, that's a nice word. Difficult. My uncle's got a bag on his side he has to empty himself, and you're sat there saying difficult like the traffic was bad.
lines.mcdonagh: You shot up my family, you're sat there orderin' veal, and you've the neck to call us difficult.
lines.houser: You sent men to my family's business with guns and now you're pitching me a partnership. Is there a brochure?
lines.coen: You shot my people. That's — I mean, that happened. That's a thing that happened and now we're eating.

lines.why: The single worst line in the scene. Two words of nothing where the audience needs to hear a man rationalize murder to a victim's face.
lines.house: Your uncle said no to me in front of people. There's no version of that where he stays standing.
lines.tarantino: It was a negotiation. Negotiations have positions. Your uncle took his position, I took mine, mine had more men in it. Don't confuse the outcome with the intent — I liked him.
lines.mcdonagh: It was business. He said no, and he said it loud, and there was a fella from Seattle watchin'. What was I meant to do, send a card?
lines.houser: That was a restructuring. Nobody enjoys a restructuring. But you don't take it personally, because the alternative is everybody gets restructured, including me.
lines.coen: Well. There was a disagreement. It got away from everybody a little. That's how these things tend to go, in my experience.

lines.why: Three words. No image, no weight. The player should make the room look at what was done.
lines.house: You shot Booski in the gut on a Tuesday and left him crawling to a payphone.
lines.tarantino: You shot Booski. In the stomach. Which — and I want you to hear this — is the one place you shoot a man when you want him to have time to think about it.
lines.mcdonagh: You shot Booski. In the stomach. Four times. He's forty-one and he shits in a bag now, so.
lines.houser: You shot Booski. He's got a colostomy bag and a lawsuit and neither one of them's covered.
lines.coen: You shot Booski. He's — he's not doing great, is the thing. It's not the kind of thing that heals up.

lines.why: Same problem — bloodless. Sal should sound almost hurt, which is what makes him frightening.
lines.house: Booski turned me down in a parking lot with his back to me. That's not a no, that's an insult with a witness.
lines.tarantino: Booski heard a very good offer, made a face, and walked away mid-sentence. Mid-sentence. Now I've got no problem with no. No is half of business. But you finish the sentence, and then you say it.
lines.mcdonagh: Booski said no. Fine. Grand. Then he laughed. And that's the bit that got him shot, if we're bein' precise about it, which we should be.
lines.houser: Booski declined a very generous package. No counter-offer, no conversation, just a hand in my face. And I'm a man who believes in consequences for bad negotiators.
lines.coen: He said no. Which is his right. But he said it in a way that — you know, there were people there. And then things went the way they went.

lines.current: Your people need to calm down.
lines.why: A hall monitor. This is a cop who takes Sal's money — he should be openly bought, openly contemptuous, and enjoying his own leverage.
lines.house: Your people need to sit down before I start finding things in their cars.
lines.tarantino: Here's my position, and I'm only in this booth because the food's free. Your people get loud, I get phone calls. I don't like phone calls. So either you take the man's money, or I start being the kind of police officer that ruins a whole family over a taillight.
lines.mcdonagh: Your lot need to calm the fuck down. I've a stack of unsolveds on my desk with your surname on 'em and a very flexible attitude to who did what.
lines.houser: Let me frame this from a law-enforcement perspective. Every one of your uncles is one traffic stop from a very long weekend, and I decide what's in the trunk when we open it.
lines.coen: Your people ought to settle down some. I'm saying that as a friend, more or less. It's not a threat. But it's not not a threat, either.

lines.why: Playground. The player is looking at the cop who broke his jaw and this is what comes out.
lines.house: You broke my jaw on a wet sidewalk while two of your guys held my arms.
lines.tarantino: You broke my jaw. Outside a hospital. With a flashlight. And then you got back in the car and finished your coffee, which is the part I keep coming back to.
lines.mcdonagh: You broke my jaw, you fat fuck. I've a plate in it. Sets off the machine at the airport.
lines.houser: You broke my jaw outside a hospital and then filed it as resisting. I've read the report. It's beautiful. You should write books.
lines.coen: You hit me. In the face. With a flashlight. I don't know that anybody's mentioned that yet tonight.

lines.why: Echoes Sal's word without meaning to; both men now sound like the same bland person. The cop's excuse should be uglier and funnier than the boss's.
lines.house: You were standing where I told you not to stand. Twice.
lines.tarantino: You were standing in a hospital corridor at two in the morning telling me about my job. In my experience, that's a conversation that ends the same way every time, and this time it ended with a flashlight.
lines.mcdonagh: You were in my way. And you'd a mouth on you. And I'd had a long day, so between the three of us, somethin' had to give.
lines.houser: You were obstructing an officer, and I want you to know I have four witnesses who'd swear to it under oath and one of them's a priest.
lines.coen: Well, you were being difficult. And I'd had a long shift. I'm not proud of it. But I'd do it again, is the honest truth.

lines.current: I want the servers, the skin market, and Wednesday nights.
lines.why: This one is actually close — the specificity is right. It just lands too clean; Sal should be greedier and more obscene about wanting it.
lines.house: I want the servers, the skin market, and every Wednesday night from now until the sun burns out.
lines.tarantino: Three things. The servers. The skin market. And Wednesdays. That's it. That's the whole list. I'm not asking for the jerky — I don't want the jerky, the jerky is a nightmare, God bless whoever handles the jerky.
lines.mcdonagh: The servers, the skins, and Wednesdays. And before you say it — no, I don't want the jerky. I've seen where it comes from.
lines.houser: I want the servers, the skin market, and Wednesday nights. That's infrastructure, retail, and footfall. Everything else you can keep, including the meat, which I want on record I have never eaten.
lines.coen: I'd want the servers. The skin market. And the Wednesdays. That's — that's the ask. I've written it down if you want to see it written down.

lines.why: Ceremonial. Reads like a motto on a crest instead of a kid defending the one night that pays for everything.
lines.house: Wednesday pays for everything. Wednesday is why my aunt has a house.
lines.tarantino: Wednesday's not a night. Wednesday's the whole thing. Wednesday is why there's a roof on my aunt's place and why nobody in my family has ever had a real job. You're not asking for a night, you're asking for the last forty years.
lines.mcdonagh: Wednesday's ours. Wednesday's been ours since before you'd a second shoe.
lines.houser: Wednesday isn't a night, it's a revenue stream, and you know it, which is why you put it last like it was an afterthought.
lines.coen: Wednesdays are the family's. That's — that's been the case a long time. Longer than you've been around, and I mean that respectfully.

lines.current: Everything belongs to someone until it changes hands.
lines.why: Fortune cookie. It is trying to be the scene's cold thesis line and instead sounds like a magnet on a fridge.
lines.house: Everything belongs to somebody right up until somebody stronger wants it. That's not philosophy, kid, that's just Tuesday.
lines.tarantino: Belongs. That's a beautiful word. My father used it about a farm in Calabria that has had six owners since he said it. Things don't belong to people. Things sit with people, for a while, until somebody with more men wants them to sit somewhere else.
lines.mcdonagh: Everything belongs to somebody. And then it doesn't. That's the whole of history, that is, and I've not even finished me drink.
lines.houser: Ownership is a story people agree to tell. And I'm here to tell you the room has stopped agreeing.
lines.coen: Well. Things belong to folks until they don't. That's about the size of it. I didn't make the rule.

lines.current: Help me, Prospect. The Sasquatches keep their territory. I get a percentage.
lines.why: The actual pitch, and it has no seduction in it. Sal is asking a kid to betray his father's house; he should make it sound like mercy.
lines.house: Help me, kid. Your family keeps the name, keeps the corners, keeps the funerals small. I take a slice off the top and nobody has to bury anybody they like.
lines.tarantino: Here's what I'm actually offering you, and I want you to hear it without your uncle's voice in your ear. Your family keeps everything. The name, the territory, the whole ugly circus. I take a percentage off the top and in exchange, nobody else in your family has to learn what a colostomy bag is. That's not a threat. That's the single most generous thing anybody has said to you this year.
lines.mcdonagh: Help me out, son. Your lot keep the lot. I take a cut. And the shootin' stops, which I'd have thought was the headline, but nobody ever leads with it.
lines.houser: I'm offering you a licensing arrangement. You retain the brand, the territory, and all the charming regional character. I take a percentage and provide what I'd call stability, which in your industry means your mother doesn't get a phone call.
lines.coen: Help me out here. You folks keep your territory. I take a percentage. Everybody goes home. It's not complicated, and I'd hate for it to become complicated.

lines.why: Fine as a beat but too small a hook for the reply it sets up; the kid can put a little teeth on it.
lines.house: How big a slice are we calling a percentage?
lines.tarantino: Percentage. Okay. See, a percentage is a number. So say the number.
lines.mcdonagh: What percentage? And don't say 'a fair one,' I'll lose me mind.
lines.houser: Define percentage. Because in my experience that word does a lot of heavy lifting for men with your job.
lines.coen: What percentage would that be? Just — ballpark. For my own information.

lines.why: The one word here that already works. Keep it; the variants only change the temperature.
lines.house: Enough.
lines.tarantino: Enough that you'll notice. Not so much you'd die over it. I've done the math on that particular line more times than you've been alive.
lines.mcdonagh: Enough. Next question.
lines.houser: A meaningful one. I'll have my accountant walk you through it, and you'll hate him, everybody does.
lines.coen: Enough. I'd rather not put a number on it at the table.

lines.current: I need to use the bathroom.
lines.why: Functional, and it telegraphs the mechanic. The Godfather beat works because the excuse is so ordinary it embarrasses the room. Give it a body.
lines.house: I gotta piss.
lines.tarantino: I need the bathroom. It's the jaw — they've got me on something for it and it goes straight through me. Two minutes.
lines.mcdonagh: I need a piss. Sorry. It's the pills for me face, they run through you somethin' shockin'.
lines.houser: I need the men's room. And before either of you says anything clever about it — yes, it's the nerves, and yes, I'd rather go now than on your upholstery.
lines.coen: I need to use the restroom. I'm sorry. It's been a lot of coffee and, you know, a lot of everything.

lines.why: Right idea, no relish. The cop is bragging about his own thoroughness one minute before it kills him — that irony should be audible.
lines.house: Go on. I checked it myself. Tank, towels, the little window. Wash your hands.
lines.tarantino: Go ahead. I checked it before you got here — cistern, towel dispenser, that little window nobody fits through. There's nothing in there but a bar of soap and your own reflection, and I'd say the soap's the friendlier of the two.
lines.mcdonagh: Off you go. I checked it meself. Twice. I'm very thorough, that's me whole personality.
lines.houser: Be my guest. I swept it personally — that's twenty-two years of policing applied to a toilet, and I want you to appreciate what that cost the taxpayer.
lines.coen: Sure, go ahead. We had a look in there already. Nothing to it. Wash your hands, though. That's just — that's just good practice.

lines.why: Serviceable but generic. It is the last order he ever gives; make it his.
lines.house: Sit your ass down, Squatch.
lines.tarantino: Sit down. You're the tallest thing in the room and it's making the waiter nervous.
lines.mcdonagh: Sit down, would you. You're loomin'. I hate loomin'.
lines.houser: Sit. You're standing like a man with a plan and it's ruining my appetizer.
lines.coen: Why don't you sit down. You're making everybody look up, and that's — nobody enjoys that.

lines.why: Two syllables of nothing at the tensest moment in the scene — the gun is not where it should be. This is where the player's panic lives.
lines.house: Come on. Come on, it's supposed to be right here.
lines.tarantino: It's supposed to be here. Behind the tank, taped, he said behind the tank. So either I'm looking at the wrong tank or somebody's about to find out how fast I can run.
lines.mcdonagh: Where is it. Where is it. He said behind the jacks. He said it twice. I'll kill him. If I live, I'll kill him.
lines.houser: It's not here. It's not here. Fantastic. Everybody in this organization can shoot a man in a fruit stand but nobody can tape a pistol to a toilet.
lines.coen: It's supposed to be here. He said it'd be here. That's what he said, and now it isn't, and I've got about forty seconds.

lines.why: Fine as a nudge; variants add the specific menace of a man who has noticed something.
lines.house: Prospect.
lines.tarantino: Kid. You went somewhere just then. Come back.
lines.mcdonagh: Are you with us? You've gone very still, and I don't like still.
lines.houser: You've drifted. And in my experience, when a young man drifts at a table like this, he's either scared or he's counting, and I'd like to know which.
lines.coen: Son? You still with us here?

lines.why: Same note twice. Escalate instead of repeating.
lines.house: Look at me when I'm buying your family.
lines.tarantino: Because I'd hate to be doing this twice. I'm not a man who enjoys saying a thing twice — ask anybody who used to work for me.
lines.mcdonagh: Am I talkin' to meself here? I might as well be talkin' to the fuckin' napkin.
lines.houser: I'm going to need engagement. This is the biggest conversation of your life and you're looking at the salt.
lines.coen: Are you hearing me? Because I've said it now and I'd rather not have said it for nothing.

lines.current: So. Do we have an understanding?
lines.why: Close to right, but it is the beat before the killing and it should feel like a hand being offered over a table with blood already on it.
lines.house: So. Do we have an understanding, or do I finish my drink and make some calls?
lines.tarantino: So. Understanding. That's the word we're using. Do we have one, or do I finish this and go make three phone calls I'd genuinely rather not make?
lines.mcdonagh: So. Are we grand, or are we not grand? Because I've a table booked elsewhere at ten and one way or the other I'm makin' it.
lines.houser: So. Are we aligned? And I want a yes or a no, not one of those beautiful family answers where nobody's said anything.
lines.coen: So. Do we have an understanding here? Because I'd like to think we do. I'd like to go home thinking we do.

lines.why: It is meant to be the lie the kid tells with a gun already in his belt. As written there is nothing under it.
lines.house: We understand each other.
lines.tarantino: I understand you completely. That's the first true thing anybody's said at this table.
lines.mcdonagh: I understand you. I do. I understand you perfectly.
lines.houser: I understand. I understand exactly what's on offer and exactly what it costs.
lines.coen: I understand. Yeah. I think I've got the shape of it now.

lines.current: Good. The Sasquatches keep their name.
lines.why: Reads as a concession being read from a list. Sal should sound generous, warm, almost fond — the last thing he ever feels.
lines.house: Good. Your family keeps the name. That's worth more than the money and your uncle's too proud to admit it.
lines.tarantino: Good. You keep the name. And don't underrate that — the name's the only thing in this business nobody can take off you with a car and four men.
lines.mcdonagh: Good man. You keep the name. Everyone loves a name. Sure the name's half the fun of it.
lines.houser: Excellent. You retain the name, the heritage, the whole beautiful folk mythology. I'm not a barbarian, I'm a partner.
lines.coen: Good. Good. You keep the name. That's important to folks, and I respect that. I do.

lines.why: The cop's last line in his life, and it is a greeting card. It should be smug, venal, and a little too pleased with itself.
lines.house: And everybody walks out of here with all their teeth. Which is more than I usually manage on a Thursday.
lines.tarantino: And everybody walks away happy. Which is rare. In twenty-two years I have been at maybe four tables where everybody walked away happy, and two of those I was lying.
lines.mcdonagh: And everyone goes home happy. Well. Happy-ish. Happy enough, which is the most anyone gets.
lines.houser: And everybody walks away happy, and I get to expense the veal. This is what community policing looks like.
lines.coen: And everybody walks away happy. That's the goal. That's always been the goal, whatever anybody says about me.

lines.current: Tell your people the business is settled.
lines.why: Correct content, no music. This is the cue the player kills him on; it wants a last beat of warmth so the violence lands.
lines.house: Go tell your people it's settled. Tell your uncle I asked after him.
lines.tarantino: Go home. Tell your people it's settled. And tell your uncle — tell him Sal asked after him. He'll make a face. Let him make the face.
lines.mcdonagh: Tell your lot it's sorted. And tell your uncle I was askin' for him. He'll not like that, which is why I'm sayin' it.
lines.houser: Take the good news home. Tell them it's settled, tell them it was amicable, and tell your uncle his health is very much on my mind.
lines.coen: You go on and tell your people it's settled. And — you know. Give my best to your uncle. Sincerely.

lines.why: The trigger line. Two words is right, but 'It is' is limp. It needs to be the last thing Sal hears and sound like a door closing.
lines.house: It's settled.
lines.tarantino: Yeah. It's settled.
lines.mcdonagh: It's sorted.
lines.houser: Consider it settled.
lines.coen: It's settled. Yeah.

scene: THE TAKE / Jerky Motel / The Beef Run
reference: THE TAKE is Heat. The Motel is a cartel buy that goes wrong. The Beef Run is contraband hauled through mountains.
diagnosis: THE TAKE has one outright doctrine violation — the Counter-Strike line winks directly at the player mid-standoff — and a debrief where a mob boss reacts to a dead civilian like a middle manager reviewing a quarter. The Motel keeps putting mission objectives in mouths ('Buy. Leave. No speeches.') and then has two different characters recite the same rulebook phrase at each other. Across all three, the Prospect answers everything in one flat word: 'Yes.' 'Why?' 'Understood.' He is the player's mouth and right now he has no tongue.

lines.current: Good thing about all that Counter-Strike I've been playing.
lines.why: CUT OR REWRITE — this is the doctrine violation. It names a real game, acknowledges the player, and tells the audience the scene is a joke at the exact moment the scene has to be a bank robbery. Everything the tone doc protects dies on this line.
lines.house: [cut it — or, if the beat is needed] Everything's slower than I thought it'd be. Why is everything so slow.
lines.tarantino: Nobody tells you it's quiet. You think it's going to be loud, and it's this. It's a man breathing through a mask and a woman's shoe squeaking on a floor.
lines.mcdonagh: It's not like I thought. In me head there was music. There's no music. There's just this fella breathin' on me.
lines.houser: Turns out the whole thing is admin. Stand here, count that, watch the door. Nobody mentions the admin.
lines.coen: Huh. It's a lot slower than you'd think. That's the part nobody mentions.

lines.why: A YouTube-intro catchphrase dropped into a heist debrief. The Shubenator wandering in is a world joke, which the doctrine allows — but he has to wander in playing his own situation straight, not doing a bit at the camera.
lines.house: Hey. Hey — is this a bad time? This feels like a bad time.
lines.tarantino: Hey. Sorry. Am I early? Because Snow said four, and it's four, but everybody's got a face on, so I'm getting the sense four was wrong.
lines.mcdonagh: Howya. Am I interruptin'? I am, amn't I. I'll come back. I'll not come back, I'll just stand here quietly.
lines.houser: Hey, guys. Big energy in here. Is this a debrief? Should I not be at the debrief? Nobody adds me to things.
lines.coen: Hey there. Everything all right? Because it doesn't seem all right, and I'd just as soon come back later.

lines.current: Armor is on. Magazines are full. I heard the plan.
lines.why: A UI status readout wearing dialogue. Nobody inventories themselves out loud. Give it the physical detail of a man about to do this for the first time.
lines.house: I'm on. Vest is on, mags are full, and my hands won't stop.
lines.tarantino: I'm ready. I've been ready for about forty minutes, which I'm now realising is a completely different thing from being ready.
lines.mcdonagh: I'm set. Vest, mags, the whole lot. And I've been sick twice, but I'm set.
lines.houser: Vest on, mags full, plan understood. And I want it on record I have never done anything like this and I am doing it anyway.
lines.coen: I'm ready. Everything's on, everything's full. I heard the plan twice. I'd hear it a third time if there was time.

lines.current: Down. Face on the floor, hands where I can see them.
lines.why: Robbery-command boilerplate. This is the kid's first time raising his voice at civilians — it should be too loud, badly pitched, and frightening because of that.
lines.house: DOWN. On the floor, face down, hands out. Nobody makes me say it twice.
lines.tarantino: Everybody down. Face down, hands flat, and look at the carpet. Look at the carpet and count. That's the whole job — you count, I count, we all go home.
lines.mcdonagh: Down! Get down! Faces down, hands out, and not one of yiz look at me. I mean it. Don't look at me.
lines.houser: On the floor. Face down, hands out, phones stay in the pocket. This is a robbery, not a live event.
lines.coen: Everybody down on the floor, please. Face down. Hands out where I can see them. Please.

lines.current: Mask is down. I can see fine.
lines.why: Pure status filler. There is a much better line hiding in what a mask actually does to a man's head.
lines.house: Mask's down. I can't hear right with this thing on.
lines.tarantino: Mask's down. And here's a thing nobody mentions — you can hear yourself. That's all you can hear. Just you, in there, breathing.
lines.mcdonagh: Mask's on. I can see grand. I can hear me own heart, which is new.
lines.houser: Mask down. Visibility's fine. Everything else about me is a work in progress.
lines.coen: Mask's down. I can see okay. It's warm in here, is all.

lines.current: Stop right there. Hands where I can see them.
lines.why: The most generic guard bark in the medium. This man is fifty-eight, unarmed by policy, and about to make the worst decision of his life.
lines.house: Hey. HEY. Don't — I'm not supposed to — just stop.
lines.tarantino: Stop. Stop right there. I want you to know I'm not supposed to engage. There's a card in my wallet that says I'm not supposed to engage. And here I am.
lines.mcdonagh: Stop where you are! Hands up! I've a card in me wallet says I'm not to do this, and here I am doin' it.
lines.houser: Stop. Hands up. I earn eleven dollars an hour and I am about to earn every one of them.
lines.coen: Hold it right there. Hands up, please. I'd rather not — let's just, let's not have this go the other way.

lines.current: First one, and you already know the answer. Somebody who came in to cash a cheque did not walk back out. That follows this family around for years.
lines.why: The content is right and the temperature is wrong. Lou is being an HR memo about a dead civilian. He should be furious in the specific way a man is furious about money and heat, which is uglier than being furious about the death.
lines.house: Somebody came in to cash a cheque and went home in a bag. That is not a robbery any more, kid. That's a murder with a bank attached, and it sits on this family for twenty years.
lines.tarantino: You know what you did. A woman came in on her lunch break to cash a cheque, and she is not going back to work. Now here's the part you're not thinking about. Nobody looks for money. Everybody looks for a body. You didn't rob a bank today. You made a bank into a place where somebody died, and that has a memory on it like nothing else in this business.
lines.mcdonagh: Some poor woman came in to cash a cheque and went out under a sheet. D'you know what that is? That's twenty years. That's twenty years of every guard in this state havin' a photo of her on a wall and your name under it.
lines.houser: A customer came in to cash a cheque and left in a bag. Do you understand what you've done to the risk profile of this entire organization? You have converted a property crime into a homicide, and homicide has no statute of limitations and no sense of humour.
lines.coen: Somebody came in to cash a cheque. And she didn't go home. That's the thing that stays. The money goes. That stays.

lines.current: Then it was a good day. Nobody hurt, everything counted, and tomorrow it is a paragraph nobody reads. Well done, kid.
lines.why: 'Well done, kid' is a little-league coach. Lou's approval should feel like being handed something heavy you cannot put down.
lines.house: Then it was a good day. Nobody bleeding, everything counted, and by Thursday it's a paragraph nobody reads. You did that. Now go home before you start liking it.
lines.tarantino: Then it was a good day. Nobody hurt, every number matched, and by Thursday it's a paragraph on page eleven that nobody finishes. You know how rare that is? I've been doing this forty years and I can count the clean ones on one hand. Go home. Sleep badly. That part never stops.
lines.mcdonagh: Then it was a good day. Nobody hurt, everythin' counted, and by Thursday it's a paragraph no one reads. Good lad. Now go home and don't be gettin' fond of it.
lines.houser: Then that's a good day. No casualties, full reconciliation, and a media footprint of one paragraph. That's not luck, that's execution. Go home, and don't let anybody buy you a drink for it.
lines.coen: Then it was a good day. Nobody hurt. Everything counted. Tomorrow it's a paragraph nobody reads. That's about as good as it gets, in this line.

lines.current: First one. I moved when Snow said move and I did not make anything worse.
lines.why: A school report card. The kid sounds meek next to Snow and Lou. He should be trying to sound calm and failing.
lines.house: First one. I moved when Snow moved. I didn't make it worse. That's all I've got.
lines.tarantino: First one. I did what Snow said, when Snow said it, and I didn't make anything worse. I keep saying that in my head like it's an achievement. I don't know if it's an achievement.
lines.mcdonagh: First one. I moved when I was told and I made nothin' worse. That's the whole of me report, so it is.
lines.houser: First job. I followed Snow, I hit my marks, and I contributed nothing anybody will remember, which I'm told is the ideal outcome.
lines.coen: It was my first one. I moved when Snow said move. I didn't make anything worse. I don't know what else you want from me on that.

lines.current: We got out. Everybody came home.
lines.why: Mission-complete recap with no adrenaline in it after a shootout and a chase.
lines.house: We're out. Everybody's home. I can't feel my hands.
lines.tarantino: We got out. Everybody came home. And I'm sitting in a car outside my own building and I can't make myself open the door.
lines.mcdonagh: We got out. Everyone's home. And I've not stopped shakin' since the second car.
lines.houser: We're out, everybody's home, and I've just realised I'm still wearing the vest.
lines.coen: We got out. Everybody came home. That's — I keep saying that. I've said it about four times now.

lines.current: Buy the meat. Leave. No speeches.
lines.why: An on-screen objective in a mouth. It is also said twice, near-verbatim, later in the scene — which is what exposes it as tutorial text.
lines.house: You buy the meat, you get in the car. You don't make friends and you don't make a speech.
lines.tarantino: Here's the whole night. You buy the meat. You get in the car. Anything you say in between those two things is a mistake you haven't made yet.
lines.mcdonagh: Buy the meat. Get in the car. And whatever you're plannin' on sayin' — don't. I can see you plannin' it.
lines.houser: Transaction, then exit. No conversation, no negotiation, no personality. You're a wallet with legs tonight.
lines.coen: You buy the meat and then you leave. That's it. No speeches. People get hurt in the speeches.

lines.why: The verbatim repeat. Fix by making the second one an escalation — he is saying it again because he can see the kid winding up.
lines.house: Buy. Leave. I said no speeches and I can see one on your face.
lines.tarantino: Buy. Leave. And I've now said it twice, which means I've seen something in you I don't like.
lines.mcdonagh: Buy. Leave. No speeches. That's twice. There'll not be a third, there'll just be me disappointed in a car.
lines.houser: Buy. Leave. And I'm repeating myself, which is a thing I do exactly once before I stop bringing somebody places.
lines.coen: Buy it. Leave. No speeches. I've said that now. I'd hate to have said it for nothing.

lines.current: Meat first. Money second. That is how this works.
lines.why: A rulebook line that Snow then parrots verbatim, making both men sound like the same laminated card. Rico should sound like he made this rule up because somebody once robbed him.
lines.house: Meat first, money second. That's not a rule, that's a scar.
lines.tarantino: Meat first. Money second. And before you tell me that's backwards — it is backwards. It's backwards on purpose, because the last man who did it the right way round is in a lake.
lines.mcdonagh: Meat first, money second. That's how it goes. Ask me why and I'll tell you about a fella in a lake.
lines.houser: Product first, payment second. Non-negotiable. I lost a lot of money learning that order and I'm not paying that tuition twice.
lines.coen: Meat first. Then the money. That's how we do it here. It's not how everybody does it. It's how we do it.

lines.current: Room twelve. Meat first. Money second.
lines.why: Snow repeating Rico's catchphrase back at him is the flattest kind of copy-paste. Snow should have his own read on the same rule, and it should be contemptuous.
lines.house: Room twelve. And he'll tell you meat first, money second, like it's scripture. Let him.
lines.tarantino: Room twelve. He's going to say meat first, money second, like he invented it. He didn't. Everybody says it. Let him have it.
lines.mcdonagh: Room twelve. He'll give you the meat-first-money-second speech. Nod along. He does love that speech.
lines.houser: Room twelve. He'll recite his little order-of-operations at you like it's a founding document. Let him finish, it's shorter that way.
lines.coen: Room twelve. He'll tell you meat first, money second. Just let him say it. He likes to say it.

lines.why: The cover story is the funniest idea in the scene and it is delivered like a stage direction. A bad lie has to be committed to, in detail, with paperwork energy.
lines.house: No. Motel inspection. County. I'm here about the ice machine and I'll be honest, I've heard things.
lines.tarantino: No. I'm motel inspection. County. And before you ask — no, I don't have a clipboard, because the county took the clipboards, which is its own scandal I'm not getting into with you in a doorway.
lines.mcdonagh: No. Motel inspection. And before you start — I know I don't look like it. Nobody looks like it. That's the whole point of it.
lines.houser: No. Motel inspection. County health, hospitality division. I'm here about the ice machine, the linens, and whatever is happening in your parking lot, which we'll get to.
lines.coen: No. I'm motel inspection. County. It's a — it's a real job. People are always surprised.

lines.why: Reads like a translation error. The joke — he refuses to sit because sitting is how you get shot — is good and is not on the page.
lines.house: I'll stand. Inspectors stand. It's in the manual.
lines.tarantino: I'll stand, thanks. An inspector who sits down isn't inspecting, he's visiting. Different form entirely.
lines.mcdonagh: I'll stand. Inspectors stand. That's the difference between an inspection and a chat.
lines.houser: I'll remain standing. Seated inspections are a different form and a different fee, and neither of us wants that conversation.
lines.coen: I'll stand, if it's all the same. That's how it's done. Standing.

lines.why: A platitude any gangster in any film could say. It is also a line the kid has not earned yet.
lines.house: That's the deal. You don't have to like the deal.
lines.tarantino: That's business. And I know how that sounds coming out of me. I've been in this eleven weeks and I'm quoting people at you. But it's still true.
lines.mcdonagh: That's business. I'm told. I've only been at it a wet week, but that's what they keep sayin'.
lines.houser: That's the arrangement. I didn't write it, I just have to stand here in a bad room and enforce it.
lines.coen: That's how it works. I didn't come up with it. But that's how it works.

lines.current: Stand where I can see you.
lines.why: Generic guard-speak from a cartel lieutenant who should sound bored, southern, and completely certain he will win.
lines.house: Stand where I can see you. And take your hands out of that jacket before I take an interest.
lines.tarantino: Stand there. Right there, where the light is. I like to see a man's hands and I like to see his shoes, and I'll tell you why some other time.
lines.mcdonagh: Stand where I can see you. And keep your hands out of that coat, you're makin' me curious and I'm awful when I'm curious.
lines.houser: Stand there where the light is. Hands out of the jacket. This is a very simple room and I'd like to keep it that way.
lines.coen: Stand right there where I can see you. Hands out. It's easier for everybody.

lines.current: Not worth it, not worth it!
lines.why: Generic panic filler with none of Rico's personality. A man who has been swaggering all scene should break in his own specific way.
lines.house: It's not worth it — it's meat, it's just meat, take the meat!
lines.tarantino: It's not worth it. Look at me. Look at what we're doing. It's dried meat. We are all going to die in a motel over dried meat.
lines.mcdonagh: It's not worth it! It's jerky! We're all goin' to be shot over jerky and I'll not have that on me headstone!
lines.houser: It's not worth it! It's a commodity! It's a low-margin commodity and none of us are insured!
lines.coen: It's not worth it. It's really not. It's meat. It's just — it's meat, fellas.

lines.why: One of a whole family of one-word Prospect responses across the Beef Run that turn the player's mouth into a dialogue-menu confirm button. Fix the pattern, not just this line.
lines.house: Yeah. I see it.
lines.tarantino: Yeah. I'm looking right at it and I still don't believe it.
lines.mcdonagh: I do, aye. I wish I didn't, but I do.
lines.houser: Affirmative, and I'd like it noted I saw it and said nothing for a full ten seconds.
lines.coen: Yeah. Yeah, I see it. Huh.

lines.current: What exactly are we picking up?
lines.why: 'Exactly' is the tell — this is a quest prompt. Make the kid ask like someone who has already guessed and is hoping he is wrong.
lines.house: What are we actually picking up? And don't say meat.
lines.tarantino: So what are we picking up. And I want you to answer that without using the word meat, because every time somebody says meat in this outfit it turns out not to be meat.
lines.mcdonagh: What are we pickin' up? And don't say meat. Every time someone says meat I end up carryin' somethin' I'd rather not.
lines.houser: What is the actual cargo? And I'd appreciate the real answer, not the customs answer.
lines.coen: What are we picking up, exactly? I only ask because it's my name on the flight plan.

lines.why: Quest-log phrasing. He should be reacting, not requesting exposition.
lines.house: How is that illegal? It's a photograph.
lines.tarantino: Explain to me how a photograph is illegal. Not a gun. Not a body. A photograph.
lines.mcdonagh: How's a photo illegal? It's a photo. Of what? Of who?
lines.houser: It's a photograph. What jurisdiction on earth makes a photograph a felony, and how much are we getting paid for it?
lines.coen: Why would that be illegal? It's a picture. I don't — okay.

lines.why: Whiny and generic for a man flying contraband through a mountain range. His panic should be competent-adjacent.
lines.house: I don't know how to do that. Tell me how to do that. Tell me now.
lines.tarantino: I don't know how. Nobody showed me. There was a whole afternoon where somebody could have shown me and instead we talked about jerky.
lines.mcdonagh: I don't know how! Nobody showed me! We'd a full afternoon and we spent it talkin' about meat!
lines.houser: I don't know how. This was not in the onboarding, and I want you to sit with the fact that there was no onboarding.
lines.coen: I don't know how to do that. Nobody told me. That's not — I'm not being difficult, I just don't know how.

lines.why: Corporate. The kid is being lectured about jerky lineage by a man who takes it deadly seriously; his answer should show he has clocked that.
lines.house: Understood. I won't say the word again.
lines.tarantino: Understood. And I want you to know I will never say that word in this vehicle again as long as I live.
lines.mcdonagh: Understood. I'll never say it again. Not once. Not even in me head.
lines.houser: Understood. Noted. Internalized. I will die before I use that word incorrectly in front of you again.
lines.coen: Understood. I won't bring it up again. That's my mistake.

lines.why: Deferential and small. He can offer without sounding like an intern.
lines.house: You want a hand, or is this a thing I'm not supposed to see?
lines.tarantino: You want a hand with that? Or is this one of those things where I help and then I know something.
lines.mcdonagh: D'you want a hand? Or am I better off lookin' at that tree for a bit?
lines.houser: Do you need help, or would helping make me a participant? Because I'm learning those are different.
lines.coen: You want a hand with that? I don't mind. I'd just as soon be useful.
